title: A half-open breaker that judges its probes as a window is proved safe and live
summary: A half-open circuit breaker used to reopen on the first probe that failed. A developer makes it judge the probes together once the last has completed, as Resilience4j does: a failed probe is recorded like any other outcome, and the failure rate of the probes decides between closing and reopening. The contract changes in three rows, the test that expected the first failure to reopen is rewritten, and the model verifies the change under both configurations: every safety invariant in every state, and every liveness property under fairness, the three that say an open breaker probes again, a dependency that comes back is used again, and a dependency that stays down gets its wait between rounds of probes. The verdict comes with what it rests on: runs of the model take one of the three rows the change alters, a failed probe before the window is complete with the failure rate at the threshold, and the other two, a failed probe with the rate below the threshold, are rows the model's two probes and threshold of one in two can never produce.

change.description: In the HALF_OPEN state, drop the branch that reopens the breaker on a failed probe, with the reasoning in a comment: the probes are judged together once the last has completed, a failed probe is recorded like any other outcome, and the failure rate decides between closing and reopening. The contract of `CircuitBreaker#decide` is regenerated: a failed probe before the window is complete now leaves the state unchanged (two rows), and a failed probe that completes the window with the failure rate below the threshold now closes the breaker (one row); a failed probe that completes it with the rate at the threshold still reopens. The test that expected the first failed probe to reopen now expects it recorded, and the breaker reopened when the probes are judged; the class comment describes the new rule.

risk: None, and that is the point. The question a reviewer has to answer is whether a breaker that lets a failed probe pass can now close too early, probe too often, or let a call through while it should be shielding the dependency, and whether, under the fairness the breaker is used with, it still probes again after it opens, still closes once the dependency is back, and still gives a dependency that stays down its wait between rounds of probes. The two examples beside this one, 075 and 077, show one-row and four-row changes of the same shape that keep every invariant and fail a liveness property. Answering by inspection means tracing the window, the probe cap and the wait through every interleaving of calls, completions and ticks; answering by model checking takes two seconds.
explanation: The breaker's rule in the model is generated from the regenerated contract, so the model runs the new rule. Under the first configuration TLC explores every interleaving of the caller, the owner, the dependency and the clock within the model's bounds, 98 states, and finds every safety invariant holding: half-open still closes only after every permitted probe, since the window must be complete before the rule closes, and still lets only the permitted number through, since the owner caps the probes whatever the rule says. Under the second it checks the three liveness properties against every infinite behaviour that respects the fairness conditions, and they hold: a failed probe no longer reopens at once, but the window completes on the next probe, and a dependency that is down fails that one too, so the rate reaches the threshold and the breaker reopens with its wait. Coverage says which rows the verdict rests on. Runs take one of the three rows the change alters, a failed probe before the window is complete with the failure rate at the threshold; no run takes the two rows of a failed probe with the rate below it, before or at the end of the window, because with two probes and a threshold of one in two, one failure in at most two is at the threshold. Those rows are live in a breaker configured with more probes or a higher threshold, and the model says nothing about them; the page says so, and a reviewer who wants them covered can widen the bounds.
resolution: Merge. The contract diff is committed with the change, and the model is checked under both configurations on every build, so the next change to the breaker is held to the same invariants and the same liveness properties.
provenance: Constructed to show an intended change to a protocol's decision rule accepted on the strength of the model, safety and liveness both, to pair with examples 075 and 077; the semantics are Resilience4j's, which judges the permitted calls of the half-open state by their failure rate.

references.title: Resilience4j, CircuitBreaker: the OPEN, HALF_OPEN and CLOSED states, waitDurationInOpenState and permittedNumberOfCallsInHalfOpenState
Nygard, Release It! (the circuit breaker pattern)
Lamport, Specifying Systems, chapter 8: liveness and fairness, and section 14.3.5, checking liveness with TLC
